item.title: Graphs with Bounded Push-Pop Walk Orderings
item.description: arXiv:2610.19724v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Consider a directed graph G and the (generally infinite) set Walks(G) of the walks in that graph. We are interested in ordering Walks(G) as w1, w2,... in a way that ensures that each walk is obtained from the previous one by a bounded number of elementary operations, namely, push operations (which add a new edge at either end of the walk) and pop operations (which remove the first or last edge of the walk). Our goal is to optimize the aforementioned bound, when it exists, in particular when imposing the additional requirement that walks must be ordered in increasing order of length. To this end, we introduce a condition on graphs inspired by earlier work, called inner-connectedness, which is testable in linear time; we show that inner-connected graphs are precisely those which admit bounded walk orderings. Focusing on such graphs, we then introduce and study the pp-rank and the pp-increasing-rank. Namely, the pp-rank of a graph is the best possible bound on the number of push-pop operations in a bounded walk ordering for that graph; and the pp-increasing-rank is the same where we further impose that shorter walks appear before longer walks in the ordering. We show that the pp-rank of inner-connected graphs is in fact always bounded by 3. The pp-increasing-rank of inner-connected graphs is also always finite, but it can be up to linear in the input graph. More precisely, we show that the pp-increasing-rank is related to a new parameter we introduce, the peripherality of graphs. In particular, for cyclic graphs, peripherality is related to the pp-increasing-rank up to multiplicative and additive constants. We last study how to compute these parameters, and show that while peripherality can be computed in polynomial time, the pp-increasing-rank itself is generally NP-hard to compute.
item.dc:creator: Antoine Amarilli, Claire David, Nadime Francis, Victor Marsault, Mika\"el Monet, Yann Strozecki

item.title: Routes planning in a condominium company using mathematical optimization
item.description: arXiv:2610.20080v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This work focuses on planning daily routes for a group of employees of a condominium company. Given a set of employees and a set of customers with pre-scheduled visits, we want to build doubly-open routes to guarantee visits to all customers, ensuring that each customer is visited by an employee with the appropriate skills to carry out the required activity. The travel times between customers and the service time in each customer are known. The problem includes time windows for visiting customers, each employee has a maximum working time, and the daily working period is between 9 AM and 6:30 PM. The routes respect the lunch break period if they extend from morning to afternoon, which means that lunch break can be avoided if the route is fully completed in the morning or in the afternoon. The aim is to minimize the distance covered by all routes with a penalty for including lunch breaks. The distances and times between customers are collected via an API to Microsoft Azure; and the solutions are then displayed on Bing Maps. The results obtained show the operational advantages of an efficient and effective vehicle routing planning in a specific condominium management company. The model can be extended to other service provider companies.
item.dc:creator: Lara Rocha, Pedro Martins

item.title: Edgewise Envelopes Between Balanced Forman and Ollivier-Ricci Curvature
item.description: arXiv:2603.13535v5 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Evaluating Ollivier-Ricci (OR) curvature on large-scale graphs is computationally prohibitive due to the necessity of solving an optimal transport problem for every edge. We bypass this bottleneck by deriving explicit, two-sided, piecewise-affine transfer moduli between the transport-based OR curvature and the combinatorial Balanced Forman (BF) curvature. We establish deterministic bounds for $\mathfrak{c}_{\rm OR}(i,j)$ parameterized by 2-hop local graph combinatorics, reducing the edgewise evaluation complexity from an optimal transport linear program to a worst-case $\mathcal{O}\left(\max_{v \in V} \operatorname{deg}(v)^{2.5}\right)$ time, entirely eliminating the reliance on global solvers. Empirical scalability benchmarks confirm these theoretical guarantees, demonstrating that the proposed transfer moduli yield significant asymptotic and constant-factor speedups over the steep polynomial scaling of exact OR evaluation. Furthermore, the tightness of these bounds is validated via distributional analyses on canonical random graphs and empirical networks, with the derived analytical bands enclosing the empirical distributions independent of degree heterogeneity, geometry, or clustering, providing a scalable, computationally efficient framework for rigorous statistical network analysis.
item.dc:creator: Giorgio Micaletto, Tebe Nigrelli

item.title: The Two-Level Poset Game is PSPACE-Complete
item.description: arXiv:2610.19558v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Poset games form a fundamental class of combinatorial games that includes classical games such as Nim and Chomp. Determining the outcome of a poset game is known to be PSPACE-complete even for posets of height at most three. However, the exact computational complexity of Two-Level Poset Game, played on posets of height at most two, has remained an open problem for over a decade. We resolve this problem by proving that Two-Level Poset Game is PSPACE-complete via a polynomial-time reduction from Avoid True on positive CNF formulas.
item.dc:creator: Kengo Hashimoto

item.title: Nonlinear fixed-distance codes via real lifts of moment configurations
item.description: arXiv:2610.19960v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Let $A_q(n,d)$ denote the largest size of a code of length $n$ and minimum Hamming distance $d$ over an alphabet of $q$ symbols. For fixed $q\ge2$ and $d\ge4$ we construct codes with redundancy $n-\log_q A_q(n,d)\le(d-3)\log_q n+O(\sqrt{\log n})$ for all large $n$. No algebraic structure is imposed on the alphabet, and the codes are not linear. For $d=4$ and $d=5$ the coefficient of $\log_q n$ matches the Hamming bound, so the redundancy is determined up to lower-order terms. At distance four the codes are provably better than every linear code: by the polynomial-method bound for cap sets, $\mathbb{F}_q$-linear codes with $q>2$ require a strictly larger coefficient in front of $\log_q n$. The construction imposes moment checksums over an auxiliary finite field, as BCH codes do, but one fewer than the distance would normally require. The affine-line theorem from prior work describes the dependencies left by these checks. We exclude them by placing the code positions inside a specially structured subset of the field, built from Behrend's sphere construction with the help of algebraic number theory.
item.dc:creator: Sergey Yekhanin

item.title: On Partial Optimality in QUBO via Quadratic Posiform Autarkies
item.description: arXiv:2610.20346v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Partially optimal assignments (also called persistencies) allow combinatorial optimization problems to be reduced by fixing a subset of variables to values consistent with at least one optimal solution. For the quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) problem, such assignments can be computed efficiently via autarkies of quadratic posiforms. However, the largest autarky domain and thus the number of fixed variables can depend on the specific posiform representation. We show that every quadratic posiform with the greatest possible constant term (the roof-dual bound) yields the largest autarky domain obtainable from any quadratic posiform. By computing such a roof-dual-optimal quadratic posiform and a corresponding autarky with largest domain in polynomial time, one can therefore attain the maximum partial optimality obtainable by quadratic posiform autarkies in polynomial time. This justifies the computation of roof-dual-optimal quadratic posiforms and corresponding autarkies in popular polynomial-time algorithms and establishes that finding additional partial optimality in QUBO requires going beyond autarkies of quadratic posiforms.
item.dc:creator: Lucas Fabian Naumann, Bjoern Andres

item.title: Potatoes and Onions
item.description: arXiv:2610.20391v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The first major step in the theory of graph minors of Robertson and Seymour was the grid theorem, a fundamental duality result describing that any graph of sufficiently high treewidth must contain a large grid as a minor. Since this pioneering work, multiple grid theorems have been established in structural graph theory, linking various width parameters of combinatorial objects with the non-existence of grid-like obstructions. In particular, Kawarabayashi and Kreutzer [STOC'15] proved a variant of the grid theorem for directed graphs that links directed treewidth with the non-existence of topological minors of large cylindrical walls. On the other hand, to study immersions of undirected graphs $-$ another containment relation that focuses on edge-disjointness, rather than vertex-disjointness $-$ Wollan [JCTB'15] introduced a parameter, tree-cutwidth, and proved that it is dual to immersions of large walls. In this work, we present a version of Wollan's parameter for directed graphs, the directed tree-cutwidth. The main result is a grid theorem for directed tree-cutwidth, establishing that it is dual to directed immersions of large cylindrical walls.
item.dc:creator: Marcin Bria\'nski, Meike Hatzel, Karolina Okrasa, Micha{\l} Pilipczuk

item.title: Claw-Free and Line Graph Edge Deletion on Block Graphs
item.description: arXiv:2610.20510v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Edge deletion problems ask for the fewest edges whose deletion gives a graph with a specified property. We study two such problems on block graphs. First making the graph claw-free, and second making it a line graph. Since every line graph is claw-free, the second problem is at least as difficult as the first. We show that on block graphs the two optimum values are always equal, and both are attained by the line graph of a forest. The main step is a completion argument, in which starting from any claw-free solution, we put back edges to get some nice structure inside each block still maintaining the claw-free property. This reduces both edge-deletion problems to the same problem of selecting vertices within the blocks of the input graph. We solve it by dynamic programming in $O(n+m)$ time, which also produces an optimal deletion set and a forest whose line graph is what remains after the completion argument. We also extend the method to $K_{1,r+1}$-free edge deletion for every fixed $r$.
item.dc:creator: Rajat Adak

item.title: Sparse universal graphs for planarity
item.description: arXiv:2010.05779v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We show that for every integer $n\geq 1$ there exists a graph $G_n$ with $(1+o(1))n$ vertices and $n^{1 + o(1)}$ edges such that every $n$-vertex planar graph is isomorphic to a subgraph of $G_n$. The best previous bound on the number of edges was $O(n^{3/2})$, proved by Babai, Chung, Erd\H{o}s, Graham, and Spencer in 1982. We then show that for every integer $n\geq 1$ there is a graph $U_n$ with $n^{1 + o(1)}$ vertices and edges that contains induced copies of every $n$-vertex planar graph. This significantly reduces the number of edges in a recent construction of the authors with Dujmovi\'c, Gavoille, and Micek.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: Journal of the London Mathematical Society, 108/4:1333--1357, 2023
item.dc:creator: Louis Esperet, Gwena\"el Joret, Pat Morin

item.title: Exploring the unleaved tree of numerical semigroups up to a given genus
item.description: arXiv:2503.14664v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We present a new algorithm for exploring or counting the numerical semigroups of a given genus that uses the unleaved version of the tree of numerical semigroups. In the unleaved tree there are no leaves rather than the ones at depth equal to the genus in consideration. For exploring the unleaved tree we present a new encoding system of a numerical semigroup given by the gcd of its left elements and its shrinking, that is, the semigroup generated by its left elements divided by their gcd. We show a method to determine the right generators and strong generators of a semigroup by means of the gcd and the shrinking encoding, as well as a method to encode a semigroup from the encoding of its parent or of its preceding sibling. With the new algorithm, we obtained $n_{76}=29028294421710227$ and $n_{77}=47008818196495180$.
item.dc:creator: Maria Bras-Amor\'os

item.title: Fundamental Limitations of QAOA on Constrained Problems and a Route to Exponential Enhancement
item.description: arXiv:2511.17259v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study the feasibility limitations of generic QAOA for permutation-constrained optimization, where valid configurations occupy an exponentially small fraction of the Boolean hypercube. Using random edge-cost TSP/ATSP ensembles, we establish high-probability bounds showing that optimized generic QAOA retains exponentially small feasible probability over specified parameter domains. At depth one, the bound holds uniformly over all mixer angles and a cost-angle grid that may be exponentially large in n^2. The analysis combines Walsh-Fourier/Krawtchouk estimates, which suppress low- and high-degree contributions, with transition-feature collision bounds controlling objective-dependent interference. Complementary cost-angle averaging, fourth-moment estimates, and light-cone analysis characterize energy-fibre coherence, typical-angle concentration, and constraint-correlation geometry. We compare generic QAOA with a constraint-enhanced kernel (CE-QAOA) initialized in a product one-hot subspace and evolved with a block-local XY mixer. For N = n^2 binary variables, CE-QAOA attains feasible probability at least n!/n^n at every depth, yielding an exp[Omega(n^2)] advantage over optimized generic QAOA at depth one with high probability. For linked cost-angle schedules with independently optimized mixer angles, the generic feasibility obstruction and exponential CE-QAOA separation extend throughout linear-depth windows p <= alpha*n, for fixed alpha > 0. These parameter-uniform bounds also imply exponential raw-sample requirements for adaptive feasible sampling within the prescribed domains.
item.dc:creator: Chinonso Onah, Kristel Michielsen

item.title: Spanning-Tree Maximization Forces Isoperimetry in the Square Lattice
item.description: arXiv:2605.23773v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We determine which connected sets of $N$ vertices in the square lattice support the most spanning trees, using all lattice edges between the chosen vertices. Every maximizer minimizes the number of edges joining the set to the rest of the lattice. Its shape is a rectangle with at most two straight strips of vertices removed at opposite corners. For $N\ge18$, the maximizer is unique up to translation, rotation, and reflection: an explicitly determined rectangle with one possibly empty corner strip removed along its longer side. The proof combines comparisons of Laplacian determinants with geometric comparisons of corner deletions. For $N=n^2$, we prove a sharp stability inequality that bounds the symmetric difference from a translated $n\times n$ square in terms of the loss in logarithmic tree count. Thus, nearly optimal tree counts force the vertex set to be close to a square. We also derive an exact product formula and a recurrence for the number of spanning trees in rectangles with a single corner strip removed.
item.dc:creator: Jiechen Zhang

item.title: Biclique decompositions from Welzl orders
item.description: arXiv:2606.09785v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: A biclique decomposition of a graph is a partition of its edges into complete bipartite subgraphs. We consider graphs whose vertices can be ordered such that the neighborhood of every vertex is the union of a sublinear number of intervals. We observe that these graphs admit compact representations in the form of biclique decompositions of small size. Here, the size of a decomposition is measured as the sum of the number of vertices of its bicliques. Combining this result with the existence of suitable vertex orderings for graphs of low neighborhood complexity, as proven by Welzl in 1988, we recover and extend several known results up to logarithmic factors. These results include upper bounds on the Zarankiewicz problem, matrix multiplication, quantum circuit complexity, and shortest path algorithms in "well-structured" instances.
item.dc:creator: Jean Cardinal, Rose McCarty, Yelena Yuditsky

item.title: Locating a Seymour vertex in oriented graphs having minimum outdegree at most 7
item.description: arXiv:2606.30588v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: A vertex $v$ of an oriented graph $D$ is a Seymour vertex if the number of outneighbors of $v$ is less than or equal to the number of second outneighbors of $v$ (vertices at directed distance exactly $2$ from $v$). Seymour's Second Neighborhood Conjecture claims that every oriented graph contains a Seymour vertex. We propose the following stronger conjecture (Conjecture 1.4): given any oriented graphs $D$, there exists a minimum outdegree vertex $s$, and a Seymour vertex $v^*$ such that the directed distance from $s$ to $v^*$ is at most $\lfloor\frac{\delta^+(D)}{3} \rfloor$, where $\delta^+(D)$ denotes the minimum outdegree of $D$. The main contribution of this article is to show that Conjecture 1.4 is true for all oriented graphs having minimum outdegree at most $7$. This, in particular, improves the results of Kaneko and Locke (2001) which (implicitly) proved Conjecture 1.4 for all oriented graphs having minimum outdegree at most $6$. In particular, this yields Seymour's Second Neighborhood Conjecture for this class of oriented graphs. We also construct a family of digraphs attaining the proposed distance bound, showing that it cannot be improved in general. Finally, by adapting existing arguments, we show that if Seymour's Second Neighborhood Conjecture is true then given any oriented graph $D$ and any vertex $v$, it is always possible to find a Seymour vertex $v^*$ such that the directed distance from $v$ to $v^*$ is at most the outdegree of $v$.
item.dc:creator: Arpan Sadhukhan, Sagnik Sen

item.title: Improved Bounds for the Bilu-Linial Conjecture via Spectral Recovery from Mixed Determinantal Polynomials
item.description: arXiv:2609.15715v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Bilu and Linial conjectured that every finite $d$-regular graph with $d \geq 2$ admits an edge signing $\sigma$ whose signed adjacency matrix $A_\sigma$ has spectral radius at most $2\sqrt{d-1}$. We prove that every signing meeting the mixed-root condition $r_{A_\sigma}\leq\sqrt{2(d-1)}$ satisfies \[ \rho(A_\sigma) < \frac{3+\sqrt5}{2}\sqrt{d-1}, \] where $r_{A_\sigma}$ is the largest root of the mixed determinantal polynomial $\chi[A_\sigma,-A_\sigma]$. The interlacing theorem of Ravichandran and Srivastava guarantees a signing satisfying the mixed-root condition, so our result improves the coefficient $2\sqrt2$ in their two-sided spectral bound. In the proof, we construct a positive matrix-valued probability measure supported on the roots of $\chi[A_{\sigma},-A_{\sigma}]$. The second moment gives a simple matrix inequality $A_{\sigma}^2 + dI \preceq 4r_{A_\sigma}^2I$, which yields a preliminary coefficient $\sqrt{7}$. Estimates for the fourth moment use information about short walks to obtain the coefficient $(3+\sqrt{5})/2$. For triangle-free graphs, the coefficient improves to $\sqrt6$, and for graphs with girth at least five, it improves to $\sqrt{35/6}$. As a result of independent interest, we extend the construction to $\chi[A_1,\ldots,A_k]$ for Hermitian matrices $A_1,\ldots,A_k$ with zero diagonal, and compute the first two moments explicitly. Finally, an explicit signing of $K_8$ shows that the mixed-root condition alone cannot guarantee a coefficient below $(4+\sqrt5)/\sqrt6$.
item.dc:creator: Fangfang Lin, Hong Zhou

item.title: Near-Optimal Online Metric Matching on $\Delta$-ary HST
item.description: arXiv:2609.25292v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In the online metric matching problem, we have $n$ servers with known locations in some metric space. Requests arrive one-by-one at certain locations, and upon arrival a request must be matched to a server that was not matched to a previous request. The goal is to minimize the matching cost. For randomized algorithms with an oblivious adversary, the best known competitive ratio is obtained by embedding the metric space into an HST, and then solving the problem in the setting where the metric space is defined by the HST. Bansal et al. (Algorithmica, 2014) introduced a framework for online metric matching where one develops an algorithm in a restricted reassignment model, and then transforms this into a true online algorithm. Using this framework, they obtained an expected competitive ratio of $O(\log n)$ for HSTs; this also gives the best known competitive ratio of $O(\log^2 n)$ for general metrics. In this paper, we revisit this framework with the aim of developing new algorithms. For HSTs where each node has at most $\Delta$ children, we develop an algorithm via this framework with an expected competitive ratio of $O((\log\log \Delta) \cdot \log \Delta)$. In particular, this ratio is independent of $n$, the number of servers/requests. It is near-optimal, as the expected competitive ratio of any algorithm is $\Omega(\log \Delta)$.
item.dc:creator: Parth Gor, Sourya Roy, Kasturi Varadarajan

item.title: Lettericity Is NP-Complete
item.description: arXiv:2609.28023v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The lettericity of a graph $G$ is the smallest size of a set $\Sigma$ such that there exist $w_1, \ldots, w_{|V(G)|} \in \Sigma$ and a so-called decoder $D \subseteq \Sigma^2$ for which $G$ is isomorphic to the letter graph $(\{1, \ldots, |V(G)|\}, \{ij : 1 \le i < j \le |V(G)|, w_iw_j \in D\})$. It took around two decades of the study of lettericity for, in the simpler case of paths, a closed-form expression for its lettericity to be derived; this suggests that the question of whether the lettericity of an arbitrary graph can be computed in polynomial time is nontrivial. Indeed, this question has been raised repeatedly as an open problem in recent literature. We solve this problem by showing that the lettericity problem on arbitrary graphs is NP-complete. We also show that each of the natural ways in which a single part of a structure $(\Sigma, w_1, \ldots, w_{|V(G)|}, D)$ witnessing the lettericity could be constrained corresponds to an NP-complete problem, which resolves an additional three open problems from the literature; in particular, we show that the coloring extension, word extension, and decoder extension problems are NP-complete. Additionally, we use the reduction in the NP-completeness proof to give a lower bound on algorithms for lettericity under the Exponential Time Hypothesis (ETH): unless the ETH is false, there cannot exist a deterministic algorithm to decide whether the lettericity of an $n$-vertex graph is at most $k$ in time $2^{o(n)}$, even when $n = 6k$. Finally, we complement the known result that Lettericity is fixed-parameter tractable when parameterized by the standard parameter $k$ by providing a fixed-parameter algorithm with respect to the dual parameterization by $n-k$ running in $2^{\mathcal{O}((n-k)^2)} + \mathcal{O}(n)$ time.
item.dc:creator: Henning Fernau, Samuel German, Kevin Mann, Nils Morawietz

item.title: Dijkstra Is NOT Greedy: A Global-to-Local Proof of Correctness
item.description: arXiv:2610.10596v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Dijkstra's algorithm is traditionally classified as a greedy algorithm. We argue that this classification misrepresents the mechanism by which the algorithm determines shortest paths. We present a direct global-to-local proof of correctness. At each iteration, the algorithm identifies a shortest path over the entire set of paths whose endpoints remain unsolved. This global minimum is necessarily a shortest path to its own endpoint. More fundamentally, the algorithm uses already determined shortest paths to establish one additional shortest path at each iteration. We identify this progression as dynamic programming. A three-step exclusion proof shows how the full path space is reduced to frontier candidates, how relaxation removes inferior alternatives, and why minimum extraction yields the global minimum. The choice is thus determined by a global comparison, not by an optimistic local greedy choice. We conclude that the algorithm is more accurately characterized by dynamic programming and deterministic path exclusion than by the traditional greedy classification.
item.dc:creator: Shengbao Wang
